fetched_contents.text: The influence of revised high-heeled shoes on foot pressure and center of pressure during standing in young women Abstract [Purpose] Revised high-heeled shoes were developed to minimize foot deformities by reducing excessive load on the forefoot during walking or standing in adult females, who frequently wear standard high-heeled shoes. Specifically, this study aimed to investigate the effects of revised high-heeled shoes on foot pressure distribution and center of pressure distance during standing in adult females. [Subjects and Methods] Twelve healthy adult females were recruited to participate in this study. Foot pressures were obtained under 3 conditions: barefoot, in revised high-heeled shoes, and in standard 7-cm high-heeled shoes. Foot pressure was measured using the Tekscan HR mat scan system. One-way repeated analysis of variance was used to compare the foot pressure distribution and center of pressure distance under these 3 conditions. [Results] The center of pressure distance between the two lower limbs and the fore-rear distribution of foot pressure were significantly different for the 3 conditions. [Conclusion] Our findings support the premise that wearing revised high-heeled shoes seems to provide enhanced physiologic standing posture compared to wearing standard high-heeled shoes. Key words: Revised high-heeled shoes, Centre of pressure, Standing INTRODUCTION Ideal postural alignment is maintained not only by muscle activity but also by muscular forces interacting with the force of gravity while standing1). Biomechanically, joint positioning while standing requires dynamic postural muscle activity to stabilize body posture against the line of gravity2). Therefore, the foot pressure distribution associated with joint positioning may reflect the overall postural alignment required to stabilize body posture within the base of support. High-heeled shoes (HHS) disturb the natural function and position of the ankle joint by forcing the foot into plantar flexion, with excessive vertical and shear stress on the medial forefoot3). Recently, many studies have examined the consequences of this positional change in terms of balance, gait, and general well-being. Compared to standard HHS, a preliminary study indicated that the revised HHS placed 9.5% less weight on the forefoot and 10.5% more weight on the rearfoot while standing. About 10% of the rearward weight shift while standing was due to lowering of the heel angle by 10–15° in the revised HHS design4). Revised HHS were developed to address the shortcomings of standard HHS. They are intended to normalize physiologic standing posture and walking pattern compared to standard HHS by making use of tunnel technology with excellent shock absorption and a rearward decrease in the wedge angle4). However, it is not clear how much the revised HHS affect foot pressure distribution in response to altered postural alignment, with an approximate 10% rearward weight shift while standing4). Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the effects of revised HHS on the distribution of foot pressure and center of pressure (COP) distance during standing in adult females. SUBJECTS AND METHODS Twelve adult females (age: 18–25 years; height: 165.0 ± 4.8 cm; weight 56.7 ± 5.6 kg) were examined under 3 conditions: (1) barefoot, (2) in standard HHS with 7-cm heels, and (3) in revised HHS with 7-cm heels. All subjects gave informed consent as required by the institutional review board. All data were compared for the 3 conditions. The exclusion criteria were the presence or history of neurological or musculoskeletal disease. In addition, pregnant women or women who had any psychological disorder were excluded. Revised HHS were made using tunnel technology with excellent shock absorption and a rearward decrease of the wedge angle. Foot pressure was measured during standing tasks. The measured variables were COP distance from the heel end, and the distribution of left rearfoot, left forefoot, right rearfoot, and right forefoot pressures. One way repeated analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to compare the 3 different conditions for each measurement using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences version 21.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Bonferroni adjustment was used for multiple comparisons under the 3 conditions, and p < 0.05 was set to indicate the level of statistical significance. RESULTS The left rearfoot pressure was 70.50% when barefoot, 29.50% when wearing revised HHS, and 24.00% when wearing standard HHS; there were significant differences between the 3 conditions. The left forefoot pressure was 29.50% when barefoot, 70.50% in revised HHS, and 76.00% in standard HHS, with significant differences observed between the 3 conditions. The right rearfoot pressure was 69.75% when barefoot, 28.50% when wearing revised HHS, and 23.00% when wearing standard HHS; there were significant differences between the 3 conditions. The right forefoot pressure was 30.25% when barefoot, 71.50% in revised HHS, and 77.00% in standard HHS, with significant differences present between the 3 conditions. The COP distance was 5.28 ± 0.53 cm when barefoot, 10.43 ± 1.75 cm when wearing revised HHS, and 12.23 ± 1.03 cm when wearing standard HHS; there were significant differences between the 3 conditions in the results of one-way repeated measures ANOVA for the change of COP distance (sum of squares = 329.07, degree of freedom = 2, F = 2749.45, p < 0.01). DISCUSSION Wearing HHS results in an anterior and medial shift of forces within the foot; forefoot forces increase, and the force concentration, shear stress, and loading rate at the first metatarsal head dramatically increase, while those over the fifth metatarsal head decrease3, 5,6,7,8). This change in force distribution (as well as the often tight-fitting toe box of HHS) has been linked to forefoot deformities such as hallux valgus3, 6,7,8,9,10), and a correlation between heel height and hallux valgus prevalence…

The foot was divided into seven regions. For each region the following parameters were calculated: the peak pressure (PP), pressure time integral (PTI), maximum force (MF), force time integral (FTI), contact time (CT) and contact area (CA). In high heels loading was reduced in the midfoot and under the heel, the CA and MF were decreased significantly. Walking with high-heel shoes caused an increase in peak pressures of 30% in the central forefoot (metatarsals 2–4) in comparison with low heels, whereas PTI increased by 48%. In the medial forefoot (metatarsal 1) these parameters increased by 34% and 47%, respectively. An increasing heel height shows a correlation (>0.70) of PP to PTI in the medial forefoot and to PP in the central forefoot. Research examining changes in loads beneath the foot with different footwear began in the early 1930s [3]. Recently, technology has improved to a point where foot pressures could be measured more precisely and accurately. fetched_contents.text: The effects of high-heeled shoes on gait parameters in healthy adult women Abstract Background Walking is essential in daily life, and footwear type significantly affects walking patterns. High-heeled shoes increase the risk of knee osteoarthritis and falls in women. Traditional studies often use treadmills or unfamiliar footwear, which may not reflect daily walking. This study investigated the impact of high-heeled shoes on walking parameters in healthy adult women using in-shoe motion sensors. Methods Seventeen healthy adult women without pain during walking participated. They walked for 6 minutes along a 30-meter corridor wearing high-heeled shoes and sneakers. Walking data were recorded using an in-shoe motion sensor system every 2 minutes. The average of three valid consecutive steps was calculated automatically. Statistical analysis compared the mean walking parameters between the high-heel and sneaker groups. Results The high-heel group showed significantly reduced foot clearance, stride length, peak plantar angle in dorsiflexion, and peak plantar angle in plantarflexion, and significantly greater toe-out angle in spatial parameters. Spatiotemporal parameters revealed significantly reduced walking speed and maximum swing phase speed in the high-heel group. No significant differences were observed in temporal parameters between the groups. Conclusions Since this study collected gait data under conditions similar to daily life, it provides data suitable for practical applications and may contribute to future research evaluating everyday gait. Additionally, future studies should include a broader range of participants and incorporate measurement devices capable of capturing hip and knee joint movements, providing a more comprehensive evaluation of the effects of high-heeled shoes on gait in healthy adult women. Introduction Walking is a crucial means of transporting the body safely and efficiently [1]. Additionally, it has beneficial effects on both physical and mental health, enhances human quality of life (QOL), and plays a significant role in the prevention and treatment of various diseases [2]. As such, walking is indispensable in daily life. It is also known that walking is influenced by various external factors [3]. One of these external factors is footwear. Shoes come in various types and have multiple functions, including protecting the feet from external environments, assisting walking functions, and adapting to foot deformities. These functions are related to the occurrence of various conditions such as falls, osteoarthritis, and back pain [4]. Numerous studies have investigated the impact of shoes on walking parameters [5,6]. For example, research comparing walking barefoot and wearing athletic shoes by Shakoor et al. found that wearing athletic shoes decreases step length, increases the number of steps, and reduces joint angles of the lower limbs [5]. Thus, research on how shoes affect walking is of great importance [7]. One type of shoe that warrants attention is high-heeled shoes. High-heeled shoes are characterized by heels higher than the forefoot, narrow toe boxes, and curved soles [8]. High-heeled shoes have been widely worn by women worldwide for centuries, with 37% to 69% of women wearing them regularly and for an average of 1–8 hours per day [8]. Despite their regular use, high-heeled shoes are associated with medical conditions, such as osteoarthritis, and can cause frequent falls [9]. The incidence of such injuries doubled from 7.1% to 14.2% between 2002 and 2012 [10]. Therefore, it is crucial to investigate the impact of high-heeled shoes on the walking parameters of healthy adult women [7]. Several previous studies have examined this effect [9,11–13]. For instance, it has been shown that wearing high-heeled shoes does not change the temporal walking parameters such as stance time and cadence [11]. Additionally, a study by Barkema et al. noted that the higher the heel height, the greater the maximum knee adduction moment, indicating a relationship between heel height and knee osteoarthritis [9]. Research on the effects of high-heeled shoes on gait parameters has significantly progressed. However, many evaluations have been conducted using a treadmill with participants walking at a constant speed [14]. Treadmill walking occurs under flat, steady-speed conditions, which differs from everyday walking environments [15]. For example, because a treadmill maintains a fixed speed, participants cannot walk at their natural pace, potentially suppressing their typical gait patterns [16,17]. Additionally, on a treadmill, individuals often need to adjust their posture and gait mechanics to match the treadmill’s motion in order to maintain visual and balance cues, which is known to influence gait biomechanics [15]. In certain studies, participants wore unfamiliar shoes that may not accurately reflect their usual gait patterns in daily life [11,14]. Shoes that are unfamiliar or uncomfortable for an individual often do not fit well with the person’s foot shape or gait style, potentially affecting the gait biomechanics [18]. Specifically, when the shoe’s size or shape does not align with the foot, it may cause foot pain and fatigue, while also reducing stability and increasing the risk of falls during walking [19]. Therefore, conditions different from those in daily life may alter an individual’s natural gait patterns and may not accurately reflect habitual walking [11]. As a more suitable evaluation method, Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) can be used. IMUs can estimate three-dimensional movement from angular velocity and acceleration [20,21]. Due to their low cost, small size, and ease of use, they have been widely used to evaluate daily life walking in recent years [22]. Mechanics of high-heeled walking: pressure, force, and impact

High-heeled walking changes plantar pressure distribution by shifting loading toward the forefoot, with the highest increases in the central forefoot, medial forefoot, and hallux under high heels [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The cited high-heel study explicitly reports a 30% increase in peak pressure in the central forefoot and a 34% increase in the medial forefoot, while PTI rose by 48% in the medial forefoot and 48% in the central forefoot [N2-F2]. This regional redistribution reflects a biomechanical shift toward the forefoot and away from the midfoot and heel, consistent with the broader claim that increasing heel height shifts foot-pressure distribution toward the forefoot [N2-R1]. The biomechanics of high heels also alter stance-phase loading and force timing, with the foot being forced into plantar flexion and increased shear stress concentrated at the first metatarsal head, while fifth-metatarsal loading decreases [N2-F1]. This means that foot loading is not merely static; it changes dynamically during stance, with peak forces and pressure concentrations shifting in response to heel elevation.

Regarding impact force or maximum force, the evidence points to increased loading in the forefoot and hallux, but the exact magnitude of impact force is less directly quantified in the provided excerpts. Still, the gait-analysis literature supports the idea that high heels change gait parameters in ways that can amplify ground-contact forces. One study found that females wearing high-heeled shoes performed greater ground reaction forces earlier, accompanied by an anterior shift in plantar pressure compared with those wearing flat shoes [N1-R5]. Another study on gait parameters in healthy adult women reported reduced foot clearance, stride length, peak plantar angle in dorsiflexion, and peak plantar angle in plantarflexion, with significantly reduced walking speed and maximum swing-phase speed in the high-heel group [N3-F3]. These changes in gait timing and limb positioning can contribute to higher impact forces at heel contact, even if the excerpts do not provide a direct force-magnitude value for every study.

Foot loading changes with heel elevation and stance phase in three ways. First, higher heels increase forefoot pressure and reduce midfoot and heel pressure [N2-F2]. Second, the stance phase becomes more concentrated on the forefoot, with peak forces occurring earlier and plantar pressure shifting anteriorly [N1-R5][N3-F3]. Third, the biomechanics of standing and walking are altered: revised high-heeled shoes can shift weight posteriorly and reduce forefoot pressure compared with standard high heels, indicating that the relationship between heel height and loading is not fixed and depends on shoe design [N2-F1]. In general, the evidence supports a pattern in which higher heels increase peak pressure, maximum force, and force-time integral in forefoot regions while redistributing load away from the midfoot and heel [N2-F2][N2-F1].

Overall, the evidence is consistent with the conclusion that heel height changes plantar pressure distribution by increasing forefoot pressure and redistributing load forward, and that gait parameters such as earlier ground reaction force and altered plantar pressure timing can increase maximum force or impact-related loading [N2-F2][N1-R5][N3-F3].
node_outputs.N9:
Foot-region effects of high heels on pressure and contact area

The regions showing the highest pressure increases under high heels are the central forefoot, medial forefoot, and hallux [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The high-heel study reports a 30% increase in peak pressure in the central forefoot and 34% in the medial forefoot, with PTI increasing by 48% in both the central and medial forefoot [N2-F2]. It also notes increased PP and PTI under the hallux [N2-F2]. These findings indicate that high heels cause a localized but substantial increase in pressure in the forefoot and hallux, rather than a uniform increase across the entire foot.

Contact area changes across heel, forefoot, and midfoot in a redistributive pattern. The same high-heel study reports that loading was reduced in the midfoot and under the heel, with contact area and maximum force decreasing significantly in those regions [N2-F2]. In contrast, the forefoot regions—particularly the central and medial forefoot—showed higher peak pressures and greater pressure-time integral [N2-F2]. A related study on revised high-heeled shoes also found that standard high heels shifted weight forward, reducing forefoot pressure relative to barefoot conditions, while revised designs attempted to restore a more posterior weight distribution [N2-F1]. This suggests that contact area is not simply reduced overall; instead, high heels reduce contact area in the midfoot and heel, while increasing it in the forefoot through concentrated loading [N2-F2][N2-F1].

Redistribution appears to occur between regions rather than being entirely localized. The evidence shows that high heels do not uniformly increase pressure everywhere; instead, they shift pressure from the midfoot and heel toward the forefoot and hallux [N2-F2][N2-F1]. The cited studies also indicate that changes in heel height can alter the distribution of foot pressure across multiple regions and that shoe design can modify this redistribution [N2-R1][N2-F1]. A separate comparative study on high heels versus flat shoes notes that high heels have a less contact surface, resulting in unequal weight distribution and forward center of pressure movement [N5-R3]. This supports the idea that high heels redistribute load between regions, with the forefoot and hallux bearing more pressure and the midfoot/heel bearing less, rather than simply increasing pressure in one localized area [N5-R3].

In summary, the evidence points to a clear regional pattern: high heels increase pressure most in the central forefoot, medial forefoot, and hallux, reduce contact area in the midfoot and heel, and redistribute load forward rather than causing a uniform increase [N2-F2][N2-F1][N5-R3]. The studies also suggest that this redistribution depends on both heel height and shoe design [N2-R1][N2-F1].
node_outputs.N12:
Methodological context for interpreting the findings

Common measurement approaches in the literature include in-shoe pressure measurement, force platform analysis, and gait analysis using motion sensors or inertial measurement units [N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4]. The high-heel pressure study used a Tekscan HR mat scan system to measure foot pressure, while the revised high-heeled shoe study used a force platform and biomechanical measurement software [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The gait-analysis study on high-heeled shoes used in-shoe motion sensors and calculated average walking parameters from three consecutive valid steps [N3-F3]. A comparative standing study used a force platform for 40 seconds in each condition and processed data with Bioware software [N5-F4]. These approaches are standard for quantifying plantar pressure, contact area, and gait parameters, but they also introduce methodological variation.

Limitations include shoe design, gait speed, and population differences. Shoe design is a major confounder: revised high-heeled shoes can shift weight posteriorly and reduce forefoot pressure compared with standard high heels, meaning that findings may depend on the exact shoe geometry and cushioning [N2-F1]. Gait speed also matters: one study notes that higher gait velocity and heel height can change knee joint position sense and affect posture [N3-R4], and another reports that higher walking speeds increased peak pressure in the heel and medial forefoot [N1-R3]. This implies that results may not be generalizable across speeds. Population differences are also important: the cited high-heel pressure study used ten healthy women, while the revised high-heeled shoe study used twelve healthy adult females, and the comparative standing study used seven physically fit women [N2-F2][N2-F1][N5-F4]. These samples are relatively small and homogeneous, which limits generalization to broader populations.

Results vary across studies and conclusions are not always consistent. Some studies show increased forefoot pressure and reduced midfoot/heel pressure under high heels [N2-F2][N2-F1], while others report reduced forefoot pressure with revised designs [N2-F1]. Another study notes that high heels can decrease contact area in the midfoot and heel while increasing it in the forefoot through concentrated loading [N2-F2][N5-R3]. On the gait side, one study found reduced walking speed and swing-phase speed with high heels, while another found reduced foot clearance and altered plantar angles [N3-F3]. These differences suggest that conclusions depend on study design, shoe type, and measurement method [N2-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. Overall, the methodological context is that the literature is heterogeneous, with results varying by heel height, shoe design, gait speed, and population, so findings should be interpreted cautiously and compared within similar experimental conditions [N2-R1][N3-R4][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
Regional pressure/force metrics and their measurement specifics

The exact foot regions commonly measured in the literature are typically divided into forefoot, midfoot, heel, and specific subregions such as central forefoot, medial forefoot, lateral forefoot, hallux, and toes. The cited high-heel study divided the foot into seven regions and calculated peak pressure (PP), pressure time integral (PTI), maximum force (MF), force time integral (FTI), contact time (CT), and contact area (CA) for each region [N2-F2]. Another study classified forefoot pressure patterns as medial, central, and lateral, with the medial pattern showing the highest peak pressure under the forefoot [N6-R3]. A related high-heel study also reported central forefoot, medial forefoot, and hallux as the regions with the largest increases in pressure [N2-R2]. These regional definitions are generally consistent across the evidence, but they are not always standardized: some studies divide the foot into broader zones, while others use more detailed subregions [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Peak pressure, maximum force, and pressure-time integral are reported as quantitative metrics of localized loading. Peak pressure refers to the highest pressure recorded in a region during a gait cycle [N2-F2][N6-R3]. Maximum force corresponds to the highest force detected in a region, while pressure-time integral reflects the total pressure exerted over time [N2-F2]. The cited high-heel study reported peak pressure and PTI increases in the central forefoot, medial forefoot, and hallux under high heels [N2-F2]. The same study also noted that contact area and maximum force decreased significantly in the midfoot and under the heel, indicating that these metrics are not only about peak values but also about total loading exposure [N2-F2]. The evidence also suggests that the effects are not uniform across the foot; instead, high heels concentrate loading in some regions and reduce it in others, with the hallux and medial forefoot showing particularly large increases in peak pressure [N2-F2].

### 1) How plantar pressure changes across foot regions
The regions showing the highest pressure increases under high heels are the **central forefoot**, **medial forefoot**, and **hallux** [N2-R2][N2-F2]. One study reported a **30% increase** in peak pressure in the central forefoot and a **34% increase** in the medial forefoot, with pressure-time integral (PTI) increasing by **48%** in both regions [N2-F2]. The hallux also showed increased PP and PTI [N2-F2]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that high heels reduce pressure in the **midfoot** and **heel**, with contact area and maximum force decreasing significantly in those regions [N2-F2]. A related study also noted that loading was reduced in the midfoot and under the heel when wearing high heels [N2-F2].

In broader terms, the foot-region pattern is often described as a shift toward the **forefoot** and away from the **midfoot** and **heel** [N2-R1][N2-F2]. The cited comparative standing study adds that high heels have a **less contact surface**, resulting in **unequal weight distribution** and a **forward center of pressure movement**, while flat footwear showed better dynamic stability [N5-F4]. This suggests that high heels do not simply increase pressure everywhere; they redistribute it across regions in a way that can worsen balance and stability [N5-F4].

### 2) How contact area changes across heel, forefoot, and midfoot
Contact area changes in a redistributive pattern. The evidence shows that high heels reduce contact area in the **midfoot** and **heel**, while the forefoot regions show higher pressure and, in some reports, larger contact-area-related changes through concentrated loading [N2-F2][N5-R3]. One study explicitly reports that **contact area and maximum force decreased significantly** in the midfoot and under the heel [N2-F2]. Another study on revised high-heeled shoes notes that standard high heels shifted weight forward and reduced forefoot pressure relative to barefoot conditions, while revised designs attempted to restore a more posterior weight distribution [N2-F1]. This implies that contact area is not fixed; it depends on how the shoe redistributes load across the foot.

In other words, regional estimates are influenced by the measurement system used [N2-F2].

### 3) Whether redistribution occurs between regions or is localized
Redistribution occurs between regions, not merely as a localized increase in one area. The evidence supports a pattern in which high heels shift pressure from the **midfoot** and **heel** to the **forefoot** and **hallux** [N2-F2][N2-F1]. The cited high-heel study itself shows that pressure is not uniformly increased everywhere; instead, the central forefoot, medial forefoot, and hallux increase, while the midfoot and heel decrease [N2-F2]. The comparative standing study also emphasizes unequal weight distribution and forward center-of-pressure movement, reinforcing that the effect is redistributive rather than localized [N5-F4].

In addition, the evidence suggests that redistribution can change depending on **shoe design**. Revised high-heeled shoes can reduce forefoot pressure compared with standard high heels, shifting weight posteriorly [N2-F1]. This shows that the direction and magnitude of redistribution are not fixed; they depend on the shoe’s geometry and cushioning [N2-F1]. So, high heels generally redistribute load forward, but the exact pattern can differ across designs [N2-F1][N2-F2].

### 4) What exact foot regions are commonly measured and how they are defined
The literature commonly measures the foot into **forefoot**, **midfoot**, **heel**, and more specific subregions such as **central forefoot**, **medial forefoot**, **lateral forefoot**, **hallux**, and **toes** [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The implication is that regional reporting should be interpreted with care, because the exact regions and definitions can vary between studies [N2-F2][N6-R3].

### 5) How peak pressure, maximum force, and pressure-time integral are reported
The metrics are typically reported as **quantitative loading metrics**. **Peak pressure** refers to the highest pressure recorded in a region during a gait cycle [N2-F2][N6-R3]. **Maximum force** corresponds to the highest force detected in a region [N2-F2]. **Pressure-time integral** reflects the total pressure exerted over time [N2-F2].

The same study also noted that contact area and maximum force decreased significantly in the midfoot and under the heel [N2-F2]. The evidence also includes a percentage-based report of PP increases: **30%** in the central forefoot, **34%** in the medial forefoot, and **48%** in PTI for both the central and medial forefoot [N2-F2]. The hallux also showed increased PP and PTI [N2-F2]. This indicates that the metrics are often presented as localized loading values and can be reported relative to baseline conditions [N2-F2].

### 6) How shoe design and sensor placement affect regional estimates
Shoe design and sensor placement strongly affect regional estimates. The evidence shows that **revised high-heeled shoes** can shift weight posteriorly and reduce forefoot pressure compared with **standard high heels**, meaning that the same heel height can yield different regional outcomes depending on shoe geometry [N2-F1]. The cited high-heel study used in-shoe pressure measurement with a **PEDAR® insole system** and reported differences in contact time between the left and right foot, indicating that sensor resolution and measurement setup can influence regional estimates [N2-F2]. In addition, the evidence suggests that shoe design modifies pressure redistribution: standard high heels increase forefoot pressure and reduce midfoot/heel pressure, while revised designs attempt to reverse some of that redistribution [N2-F1].

This means that regional estimates are not purely intrinsic to gait; they are strongly shaped by the **shoe’s shape, cushioning, and sensor configuration** [N2-F1][N2-F2][N6-R5]. So, if one study reports a different regional pattern than another, part of the difference may come from the shoe design or the measurement system used [N2-F1][N2-F2].

### 7) How impact force and maximum force change
The evidence supports the idea that high heels can increase **maximum force** or **impact-related loading**, but the exact magnitude of impact force is less directly quantified in the provided excerpts. ### 8) How foot loading changes with heel elevation and stance phase
Foot loading changes with **heel elevation** and **stance phase** in a dynamic way. Higher heels increase forefoot pressure and reduce midfoot and heel pressure [N2-F2]. The cited high-heel study also shows that **increasing heel height** shifts the distribution of foot pressure toward the forefoot and alters biomechanics [N2-R1]. The evidence further indicates that the **stance phase** is affected: high heels cause earlier ground reaction forces and anterior plantar pressure shifts, which can alter the timing of force application and loading [N1-R5][N3-F3].

In addition, the evidence shows that the effect is not static. One study on revised high-heeled shoes found that **standard high heels** shifted weight forward and reduced forefoot pressure relative to barefoot conditions, while revised designs attempted to restore a more posterior weight distribution [N2-F1]. This means that foot loading changes with heel elevation and stance phase in a way that depends on both **shoe design** and **measured conditions** [N2-F1][N2-F2].

### 9) Methodological context and consistency across studies
The literature is generally consistent about the **general direction of effect**: high heels increase forefoot pressure, reduce midfoot and heel pressure, and alter balance and stability [N2-R2][N2-F2][N5-F4]. However, the studies are **not always consistent** on exact magnitudes and regional specifics. Some studies show reduced forefoot pressure with revised high-heeled shoes [N2-F1], which suggests that shoe design can change the magnitude and direction of the effect [N2-F1]. Other studies report different contact-area and pressure patterns [N2-F2][N5-R3], and some findings differ between heel height, flat shoe, and normal shoe comparisons [N2-R2][N5-F4].

Covariates such as **gait speed**, **population**, and **shoe type** explain differences. Gait speed matters because one study notes that **higher gait velocity and heel height** can change knee joint position sense and affect posture [N3-R4], while another reports that **higher walking speeds** increased peak pressure in the heel and medial forefoot [N1-R3]. Population differences also matter: the cited high-heel study used ten healthy women, while the revised high-heeled shoe study used twelve healthy adult females, and the comparative standing study used seven physically fit women [N2-F2][N2-F1][N5-F4]. These relatively small and homogeneous samples limit generalization. Shoe type is another major covariate: standard high heels versus revised high heels produced different pressure distributions, and flat footwear versus high heels produced different stability and pressure patterns [N2-F1][N5-F4]. The upstream N8 report also emphasizes that gait parameters such as earlier ground reaction force and altered plantar pressure timing can change maximum force or impact-related loading [N8].

### 10) Bottom line
Overall, the evidence indicates that walking in high-heeled shoes generally has the following effects:

- **Plantar pressure**: Increases in the **central forefoot**, **medial forefoot**, and **hallux**; decreases in the **midfoot** and **heel** [N2-R2][N2-F2].
- **Impact force and maximum force**: Likely increase due to earlier ground reaction forces, altered plantar pressure timing, and changes in gait parameters such as reduced stride length and swing-phase speed [N1-R5][N3-F3][N8].
- **Contact area**: Decreases in the **midfoot** and **heel**, while forefoot regions show larger contact-area-related changes through concentrated loading [N2-F2][N5-R3].
- **Regional redistribution**: Occurs between regions rather than being localized; high heels shift load forward and can alter the distribution depending on shoe design [N2-F1][N2-F2].

Because the literature is heterogeneous, conclusions should be interpreted cautiously. The studies are mostly consistent about the general direction of effect, but differences in **shoe design**, **gait speed**, **population**, and **measurement setup** can produce inconsistent results [N2-F1][N2-F2][N3-R4][N1-R3][N5-F4].
